overview: Quaesitosaurus (meaning 'extraordinary lizard') was a large herbivorous sauropod from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia, tentatively dated to approximately 86–72 million years ago, though the precise range is uncertain. Named by Kurzanov and Bannikov in 1983, it is estimated to have reached around 23 metres in length and is known only from a partial skull—primarily the back of the braincase and lower jaws—from the Baruungoyot Formation of Omnogov province. It belongs to Nemegtosauridae within Diplodocoidea.

Quaesitosaurus is one of two Mongolian nemegtosaurids known primarily from skulls (the other being Nemegtosaurus), and its skull shows a diplodocid-like elongated snout with pencil-shaped teeth suited for cropping vegetation. Its partial skull has been studied for evidence of inner ear morphology, suggesting it may have had good low-frequency hearing—possibly an adaptation for long-range communication in a social sauropod.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Quaesitosaurus orientalis was named by Kurzanov and Bannikov in 1983 from a partial skull collected in the Baruungoyot Formation. The species name refers to its eastern provenance (Mongolia). It was one of several sauropod discoveries to emerge from Soviet-Mongolian expeditions to the Gobi Desert during the 1970s–1980s.

articles.title: Skull Morphology
articles.body: The known cranial material includes the occiput, parts of the braincase, and lower jaw elements. These show the characteristic features of Nemegtosauridae: a long, slender skull with pencil-like teeth at the front of the jaws—a diplodocoid-style skull that contrasts markedly with the more robust skulls of titanosaurs found in the same deposits.

articles.title: Hearing and Communication
articles.body: Analysis of the inner ear region of the Quaesitosaurus skull has suggested a cochlear morphology suited to low-frequency sound detection. If accurate, this may indicate that large Mongolian sauropods were capable of sensing or producing infrasound, possibly for long-distance communication between herd members—though these interpretations are speculative.

articles.title: Relationship to Nemegtosaurus
articles.body: Some researchers have suggested that Quaesitosaurus and Nemegtosaurus may represent the same animal at different ontogenetic stages or from different parts of the skeleton of the same genus. This has not been conclusively demonstrated, and both are currently retained as separate genera pending discovery of more complete material.

record.mya: late Campanian, about 75-72 million years ago
record.description: Quaesitosaurus orientalis is a titanosaur from the Baruungoyot Formation of Mongolia, based almost entirely on one incomplete skull.
facts: The type skull has the elongate muzzle and slender teeth associated with nemegtosaurid titanosaurs.
Postcranial anatomy, total length and armour are unknown for the type.
Its distinction from Nemegtosaurus has been questioned but cannot be resolved confidently from current material.

review.ageReviewNote: The type comes from the late Campanian Baruungoyot Formation; it should not be assigned the age of the younger Nemegt Formation.
